findings.issue_text: [BUG] The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` in test_basic is a no-op because the test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so the flusher thread never receives the wall-clock time the comment claims to give it. The test's intended synchronization between the drift change and the flusher threads never happens; the test relies on the flusher thread being scheduled by luck, producing intermittent/flaky failures in CI (the flusher may not have flushed the segment before step.join() asserts on `messages`).

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is dead code: no call site in this diff or its tests exists; every restart path goes through `_create_processes`/`_ensure_processes_alive` which call `_create_process_for_shards` directly. The next maintainer changing restart logic must reason about two near-identical methods, and a future caller of the singular variant would silently restart a process for a shard and overwrite `self.processes[process_index]` without killing the old one, leaking a process. Deleting the method removes the ambiguity entirely.

[ADVISORY] The `if not process: continue` guard in `_ensure_processes_alive` can never trigger, because `self.processes` is only ever populated with live objects returned by `make_process(...)` immediately after construction. Readers assume processes can be None and that some path leaves empty slots, obscuring the actual invariant; if a process dies it is still present and `is_alive()` returns False, which is handled below. The guard should be deleted.

[ADVISORY] `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` combined with `max_processes or len(...)` means a `--flusher-processes 0` value silently degrades to one process per shard (the maximum), inverting the operator's intent. An operator setting `--flusher-processes 0` expecting to disable the multi-process flusher instead spawns the largest possible number of Redis-connected flusher processes, one per shard, multiplying COGS and Redis connections on a path that was previously single-process.

[BUG] The test's time.sleep(0.1) 'give flusher threads time' synchronization is a no-op because monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None) patches the global time.sleep that the test itself calls. test_basic races the flusher threads without any actual waiting, producing intermittent failures where messages is empty; the new sleep line gives false confidence that the drift-change path is covered deterministically.

[BUG] When flusher_processes is None (the factory default, i.e. any deployment not passing the new --flusher-processes flag), max_processes becomes len(buffer.assigned_shards) and the flusher spawns one process per shard instead of the previous single flusher process. Existing consumers upgraded without the new CLI option go from 1 flusher process to N (one per assigned shard, potentially dozens), multiplying spawn cost, Redis connections, and memory; the help text 'Defaults to 1' describes only the click default, not the factory default.

[ADVISORY] submit() now performs len(self.buffers) calls to record_stored_segments() and, when max-memory-percentage < 1.0, len(self.buffers) calls to get_memory_info() per submit, where the old code made exactly one of each on the shared buffer. Operators raising flusher-processes see per-message Redis round-trips and memory-info fetches scale linearly with process count on the consumer's submit path; the single-buffer implementation amortized this to one call.

[ADVISORY] No test in the diff covers the health-monitoring/restart path — _ensure_processes_alive's hang detection (max-unhealthy-seconds), the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError, per-process restart via _create_process_for_shards, or the exitcode 'no_process_' cause — which is the feature named in the PR title. A regression in the restart loop (e.g. the new per-process restart counter or the kill/ValueError handling) ships undetected; the only restart-related test coverage is the pre-existing backpressure assertion in test_flusher.py.

[ADVISORY] max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) treats an explicit flusher_processes=0 from the CLI as falsy and silently expands to one process per shard, contradicting the 'Maximum number of processes' help text. An operator setting --flusher-processes 0 expecting to disable or minimize parallelism gets the maximum possible process count instead, with no validation error.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code: no call site exists anywhere in this diff or its tests, so it is implementation work traceable to no requirement. Future maintainers assume per-shard restart is wired up and call it, but it restarts the whole shared process for that shard and is never exercised by any test, so it will bit-rot and mask the actual restart path _ensure_processes_alive uses.

[ADVISORY] The two timers use inconsistent metric tag keys — spans.buffer.flusher.produce tags {"shard": shard_tag} while spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce tags {"shards": shard_tag} — a drift introduced by this diff that breaks the metric family. Anyone building dashboards/queries on the flusher produce path gets split series depending on which timer they look at, and the existing untagged spans.buffer.flusher.produce series silently disappears (replaced by high-cardinality per-shard tags), breaking existing alerts on the old metric name.

[ADVISORY] The isinstance-vs-hasattr documentation example in CLAUDE.md is unrelated to the stated PR intent (span buffer multiprocess enhancement with health monitoring) and is not traceable to any requirement in this PR. Reviewers and archaeologists grepping this PR for the flusher change will find an unrelated style-guide edit mixed in, polluting the change's traceability; if the rule needed documenting it belongs in its own commit.

[ADVISORY] max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) silently discards an explicitly-configured value of 0, expanding to one process per shard instead of honoring the configured cap. An operator setting --flusher-processes 0 intending to disable/limit flushing gets the maximum process count (up to one process per shard) with no warning, since options are handled in the new submit() path without validating the click option.

[ADVISORY] submit() now emits metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure") once per backpressured process per submit call instead of once, inflating the counter by the number of processes whenever more than one flusher is backpressured. Operators relying on the backpressure metric's rate to gauge severity see N-times-inflated counts under the multi-process default, distorting alerting thresholds the moment flusher_processes > 1 ships.

[BUG] On the threading path (produce_to_pipe mode), a hung flusher thread is never terminated before a replacement is started, so two threads poll the same shards and produce duplicate spans. `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False for Thread, so the kill is skipped; `_create_process_for_shards` starts a new thread for the same shard list while the hung 'unhealthy' one is still alive, and both poll Redis and produce the same segments to Kafka — downstream consumers get duplicated span payloads, and repeated hang-restarts accumulate hung threads.

[ADVISORY] When `flusher_processes` is None (the default for every other construction path), `max_processes` defaults to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, silently changing the historical behavior of one flusher process to one spawn process per shard. Operators deploying this without setting `--flusher-processes` get N spawned Python interpreters (each with its own Kafka producer) per consumer where they had one, multiplying memory and Redis/Kafka connection count by shard count — a resource cliff invisible until it hits pod limits.

[BUG] The `time.sleep(0.1)` added to 'give flusher threads time to process' is monkeypatched to a no-op by the `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top of the same test, so the test passes without actually waiting. The test exercises a race between the drift update and the background thread, and it goes green without the wait it claims to perform — a stand-in guard that can stay green while the production race exists; any refactor that lengthens the race window will not be caught.

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is dead code — no caller anywhere in the diff or the strategy calls it. The next maintainer hunting restart logic finds two near-identical restart entry points and must determine which is real; the dead one also can't restart a shared process correctly (it would double-assign), so leaving it invites a wrong future call site.

[BUG] The two flusher timers use inconsistent tag keys ('shard' vs 'shards') for the same shard identity. Any dashboard/alert querying spans.buffer.flusher.produce by tag 'shard' misses the wait_produce series querying 'shards', so operators tracking per-shard produce latency see split/incomplete data after this deploy.

[BUG] join() breaks out of the process loop when the deadline expires and only terminates processes it actually waited on, so remaining flusher processes are never terminated. On shutdown with a short timeout and multiple processes, processes after the first un-waited index keep running (or leak as live spawns) after join() returns, unlike the old single-process path which unconditionally terminated; the consumer shuts down with orphaned flusher processes still polling Redis.

[BUG] The added time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep to a lambda returning None, so the flusher thread gets zero guaranteed time to process after the drift change. test_basic intermittently fails in CI: the flusher thread races the main thread's step.join() with no actual wait, producing flaky failures exactly like the flakiness this sleep was presumably meant to fix.

[ADVISORY] max_processes=0 (a plausible CLI misconfiguration of --flusher-processes) is silently coerced to 'all shards' by the `max_processes or len(...)` idiom, inverting the operator's intent. An operator setting --flusher-processes 0 to disable the flusher instead gets one process per shard, silently changing resource usage in the opposite direction of the configured value.

[ADVISORY] The entire _ensure_processes_alive restart path (crash detection, per-process restart counter, RuntimeError after MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS, hang detection) has no test coverage in this diff despite being the core of the 'Health Monitoring' in the PR title. A regression in restart logic — e.g. the new isinstance-based kill guard or per-process restart counter — ships undetected; the next engineer changing this code has no executable spec of the health/restart contract.

[ADVISORY] submit() now calls record_stored_segments() on every per-shard SpansBuffer on every submit, replacing a single call on the shared buffer, without any test asserting the aggregate semantics match the previous single-buffer accounting. If record_stored_segments maintains per-instance state (Redis counters keyed per buffer instance), the restart path in _create_process_for_shards constructs a fresh SpansBuffer that is swapped into self.buffers, dropping that process's accumulated accounting mid-stream; whoever debugs drift/count metrics gets bitten by silently reset counters after each restart.

[ADVISORY] The backpressure MessageRejected check now raises when ANY process exceeds the threshold but the metrics.incr fires once per exceeded process per submit call, changing the metric's emission rate versus the single-process baseline. Existing dashboards/alerts on spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure rate will see N-times-higher counts for the same incident once flusher_processes > 1, tripping rate-based alerts without any alerting change.

[BUG] join() waits sequentially on each process against a shared absolute deadline and breaks out of the loop without terminating or waiting for the remaining processes once the deadline passes. With N flusher processes and a join timeout T, the first slow process consumes the entire T; all subsequent processes are skipped via `break` and never receive terminate(), so spawned processes/thread flushers stay alive past shutdown and any in-flight segments in their shards are dropped — a consumer restart loses data. No test in the diff exercises join() with more than the fast path, so this is unverified.

[BUG] The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` in test_basic is a no-op because the test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top of the function, so the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is false and no waiting actually happens. The test passes by racing luck rather than by synchronization: if the flusher threads haven't produced the segment when assertions run, the test flakes; reviewers reading the comment believe the sleep covers the new multiprocess handoff. Note the patched lambda ignores its argument, but it still replaces module-level time.sleep, including this new call.

[ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit is a structural mirror test: it asserts `flusher.num_processes == 2` and `flusher.max_processes == 2` (echoes of the constructor argument it just passed), never submits or polls a message, and ends with step.join() having verified zero output. The test passes even if the multi-process shard mapping is broken (e.g., shards assigned to the wrong processes, a process flushing nothing, or processes double-flushing a shard) because no behavioral assertion exists — a regression in shard routing or per-process flushing is invisible to it. The only structural check that has any content is total_shards == 4, which is also derivable from the input.

[ADVISORY] The entire rewritten restart path in _ensure_processes_alive — the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError raise, the kill-and-recreate of a shard-group process, and the new per-shard `flusher_unhealthy` metric emission — has no test in the diff that triggers it (no process is killed, no hang simulated, no restart counter incremented in either test file). The highest-risk new logic in the diff (per-process restart bookkeeping, the kill()/isinstance guard, replacing entries in self.processes/self.buffers) ships unverified; checked tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py and test_consumer.py — neither kills a process nor manipulates process_healthy_since. A regression here silently breaks crash recovery in production.

[ADVISORY] The backpressure check in submit() now loops over per-process backpressure Values and was verified only by the single-process test_flusher.py assertion `any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())`, which does not distinguish per-process isolation — a backpressure flag stuck on a dead process's Value (whose owning process was replaced but the old Value object kept via process_to_shards_map recreation gap) would still trip the any(). Specifically, when a process is restarted, _create_process_for_shards writes a fresh healthy/backpressure Value into process_healthy_since/process_backpressure_since but nothing ever zeroes the old backpressure Value passed to the killed process; a killed process that had set backpressure_since > 0 leaves a stale Value that permanently raises MessageRejected after backpressure-seconds elapse, and no test covers a restart followed by continued submission.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code — no caller in the diff or retained code paths invokes it (restarts go through _create_process_for_shards directly via _ensure_processes_alive). The next maintainer changing shard-to-process mapping must reason about two near-duplicate creation paths; it also performs the wrong restart granularity (restarts one shard's process rather than the whole process group). Deletion candidate.

[BUG] The shard-to-process mapping is computed once from buffer.assigned_shards at construction and never updated, so shards added by a Kafka rebalance are never polled by any flusher process. After a partition rebalance that assigns new partitions to this consumer, spans for the new shards are written to Redis but no flusher process ever polls them; segments accumulate in Redis until memory backpressure rejects all messages — silent data stall/loss for those shards until the consumer is restarted.

[BUG] When buffer.assigned_shards is empty, num_processes is min(max_processes, 0) = 0, so zero flusher processes are created and the flusher has no worker at all. A consumer instantiated with no assigned partitions creates no processes; if partitions are subsequently assigned (the rebalance gap above), there is no flusher to drain Redis, and _ensure_processes_alive iterates an empty dict so no restart/health check ever fires.

[BUG] _create_process_for_shard restarts a process by calling _create_process_for_shards, which spawns a brand-new process and overwrites self.processes[process_index] without joining or reaping the dead/killed old process object, and it is also never called from anywhere (dead code diverging from the restart path in _ensure_processes_alive). Maintainers calling this helper (its name suggests the per-shard restart entry point) get a duplicate process for the same shards alongside the one _ensure_processes_alive manages, causing double-flushing of the same Redis segments and double-producing spans to Kafka; at minimum it is dead code whose presence signals the restart design was left half-refactored.

[ADVISORY] join(timeout) consumes the shared deadline across the per-process loop and breaks out on expiry without terminating the remaining processes. On shutdown with a timeout, processes later in the dict are left running (never .terminate()d) while join returns; in the produce_to_pipe=None spawn path those child processes linger holding Redis connections, and any segments still buffered in those shards are never flushed before the consumer exits.

[ADVISORY] The health-check branch `if not process: continue` is a dead guard — dict values are always Process/Thread objects, never falsy — so the intended 'no process for this index yet' condition it appears to protect against cannot fire. A future refactor that leaves a slot empty (e.g. failed spawn storing None) will silently skip health monitoring for that index with no restart attempted, leaving shards unflushed while the consumer reports healthy.

[BUG] The restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` only kills `multiprocessing.Process` instances; when `produce_to_pipe` is set the flusher runs as a `threading.Thread`, and a hung thread is left running while `_create_process_for_shards` immediately starts a replacement on the same shards. Two threads poll Redis for the same shards concurrently, so segments can be flushed/produced twice or torn between the old and new thread; the 'unhealthy' condition that triggered the restart is never actually cleared in thread mode, so every subsequent submit() spawns yet another duplicate thread until MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS raises RuntimeError.

[BUG] `join()` breaks out of the process loop when the deadline expires, skipping `process.terminate()` for all remaining processes. On a consumer shutdown where the first process eats the whole join timeout, every remaining flusher process is never terminated and is left running after the consumer's strategy is considered shut down, holding Redis connections and potentially producing duplicate spans; the old single-process code always called terminate after the wait loop.

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code that starts a new process for a shard's group without killing or joining the existing process stored in `self.processes[process_index]`. Any future caller of this helper (its name invites use in per-shard health handling) silently double-assigns shards to two live processes; the next change to restart logic that reaches for this method introduces duplicate flushing with no error surfaced.

[ADVISORY] The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer uses tag key `"shards"` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` use `"shard"`, both carrying the same `shard_tag` value. Operators dashboarding flusher latency split by shard get wait_produce split into a separate series key from produce, fragmenting the metric family and making the wait-vs-produce comparison silently unjoinable per shard.

[ADVISORY] The restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` builds a brand-new `SpansBuffer(shards)` and overwrites `self.buffers[process_index]`, dropping the old buffer object (and its Redis connection pool) without closing it, and every restart repeats this. A consumer experiencing repeated flusher restarts (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process) leaks one Redis connection pool per restart per process; under the crash-loop conditions this code exists for, the leak compounds exactly when Redis is already under pressure.

goldens.comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` but nothing in the shown code or tests calls it; restarts are handled in `_ensure_processes_alive()` which kills (for `multiprocessing.Process`) and then calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. As written, `_create_process_for_shard` would restart a process by calling `_create_process_for_shards` without first killing/terminating an existing process for that `process_index`, which could leak a running process if it were ever used. This is a maintainability/ambiguity issue grounded in the diff, but not an active runtime defect since it’s currently unused.

adjudication.rationale: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the loop starts with `for process_index, process in self.processes.items():` followed by `if not process: continue`. In this diff, `self.processes` is only populated in `_create_process_for_shards` with `process = make_process(...); process.start(); self.processes[process_index] = process`, and there is no code shown that ever assigns `None` (or any other falsy value) into `self.processes`. Since `multiprocessing.Process`/`threading.Thread` objects are truthy even when dead, the guard is redundant and may misleadingly suggest `self.processes` can contain empty slots.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats an explicit `max_processes=0` as falsy and replaces it with `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. Then `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` yields one process per shard. Since the new Click option `--flusher-processes` is `type=int` with no validation preventing 0, the diff verifiably makes `--flusher-processes 0` invert intent and spawn the maximum number of flusher processes.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and then `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`, which means when `max_processes` is `None` it becomes `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and the flusher will create `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` processes via `_create_processes()`/`_create_process_for_shards()` (one per shard). Previously the flusher created a single background worker (`self._create_process()` and stored it in `self.process`). `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` sets `flusher_processes: int | None = None` by default and passes it through as `max_processes=self.flusher_processes`, so any call site that constructs the factory without explicitly passing `flusher_processes` will now default to spawning one process per assigned shard, contradicting the new CLI help text that says it defaults to 1.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] submit() now performs len(self.buffers) calls to record_stored_segments() and, when max-memory-percentage < 1.0, len(self.buffers) calls to get_memory_info() per submit, where the old code made exactly one of each on the shared buffer. Operators raising flusher-processes see per-message Redis round-trips and memory-info fetches scale linearly with process count on the consumer's submit path; the single-buffer implementation amortized this to one call.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows SpanFlusher.submit() changed from a single shared buffer call to iterating over per-process buffers: it now does `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): buffer.record_stored_segments()` and, under `max_memory_percentage < 1.0`, it builds `memory_infos` by `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` (src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py). This makes Redis-related work and memory-info fetching scale with the number of flusher processes/buffers, whereas previously it was exactly one call on `self.buffer`. That’s a real, diff-grounded performance/scaling concern rather than a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test in the diff covers the health-monitoring/restart path — _ensure_processes_alive's hang detection (max-unhealthy-seconds), the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError, per-process restart via _create_process_for_shards, or the exitcode 'no_process_' cause — which is the feature named in the PR title. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) treats an explicit flusher_processes=0 from the CLI as falsy and silently expands to one process per shard, contradicting the 'Maximum number of processes' help text. An operator setting --flusher-processes 0 expecting to disable or minimize parallelism gets the maximum possible process count instead, with no validation error.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, the diff sets `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. Because `0` is falsy, an explicit `flusher_processes=0` (which the new Click option `type=int` does not prevent) will be treated the same as `None` and replaced with `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, i.e., the maximum parallelism. This is a concrete behavior mismatch introduced by the diff and should be handled via explicit `None` checking and/or input validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code: no call site exists anywhere in this diff or its tests, so it is implementation work traceable to no requirement. Future maintainers assume per-shard restart is wired up and call it, but it restarts the whole shared process for that shard and is never exercised by any test, so it will bit-rot and mask the actual restart path _ensure_processes_alive uses.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py`, the diff introduces `def _create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int):` (singular) but there is no call site shown anywhere in the diff (restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive` uses `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The two timers use inconsistent metric tag keys — spans.buffer.flusher.produce tags {"shard": shard_tag} while spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce tags {"shards": shard_tag} — a drift introduced by this diff that breaks the metric family. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) silently discards an explicitly-configured value of 0, expanding to one process per shard instead of honoring the configured cap. An operator setting --flusher-processes 0 intending to disable/limit flushing gets the maximum process count (up to one process per shard) with no warning, since options are handled in the new submit() path without validating the click option.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, the line `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` will treat an explicitly provided `max_processes=0` as falsy and replace it with `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, effectively expanding to one process per shard rather than honoring the configured cap. The new click option `--flusher-processes` is `type=int` with no validation in the diff, so `0` is a valid CLI value that would trigger this silent behavior change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] submit() now emits metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure") once per backpressured process per submit call instead of once, inflating the counter by the number of processes whenever more than one flusher is backpressured. Operators relying on the backpressure metric's rate to gauge severity see N-times-inflated counts under the multi-process default, distorting alerting thresholds the moment flusher_processes > 1 ships.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.submit()`, backpressure checking was changed to iterate `for backpressure_since in self.process_backpressure_since.values():` but the code still does `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure")` immediately followed by `raise MessageRejected()` inside the loop. Because the exception exits `submit()` on the first backpressured process encountered, the counter can increment at most once per `submit()` call, not once per backpressured process. The claimed N-times inflation with `flusher_processes > 1` is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] On the threading path (produce_to_pipe mode), a hung flusher thread is never terminated before a replacement is started, so two threads poll the same shards and produce duplicate spans. `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False for Thread, so the kill is skipped; `_create_process_for_shards` starts a new thread for the same shard list while the hung 'unhealthy' one is still alive, and both poll Redis and produce the same segments to Kafka — downstream consumers get duplicated span payloads, and repeated hang-restarts accumulate hung threads.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive`, when a worker is deemed unhealthy (`hang`) or dead, it unconditionally starts a replacement via `_create_process_for_shards(...)`. But the termination logic only executes for `multiprocessing.Process` (`if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()`), so in the `produce_to_pipe is not None` path (where workers are `threading.Thread`), the unhealthy thread is not stopped/terminated before a new thread for the same shard set is started. This is directly shown by the thread creation in `_create_process_for_shards` (`make_process = threading.Thread`) and the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` which does not signal/stop the prior thread. That can lead to multiple concurrently running flusher threads for the same shards and repeated restarts accumulating threads; whether it causes duplicate Kafka production depends on `SpansBuffer`/Redis semantics not shown here, but the “never terminated before replacement” and “restart accumulates threads” defect is verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] When `flusher_processes` is None (the default for every other construction path), `max_processes` defaults to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, silently changing the historical behavior of one flusher process to one spawn process per shard. Operators deploying this without setting `--flusher-processes` get N spawned Python interpreters (each with its own Kafka producer) per consumer where they had one, multiplying memory and Redis/Kafka connection count by shard count — a resource cliff invisible until it hits pod limits.

adjudication.rationale: The diff verifiably changes the default concurrency model: `SpanFlusher.__init__` now sets `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and then `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`, which means when `max_processes` is `None` (the default path via `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory(flusher_processes: int|None=None)` and `max_processes=self.flusher_processes`), it will spawn `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` processes/threads instead of the prior single `self.process` created by `_create_process()`. This is a significant operational/behavioral change (resource scaling with shard count) but not a correctness defect per se, and the updated docstring explicitly states “Creates one process per shard,” suggesting intent; the review concern is about the surprising default/backwards-compat/resource cliff rather than a functional bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The `time.sleep(0.1)` added to 'give flusher threads time to process' is monkeypatched to a no-op by the `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top of the same test, so the test passes without actually waiting. The test exercises a race between the drift update and the background thread, and it goes green without the wait it claims to perform — a stand-in guard that can stay green while the production race exists; any refactor that lengthens the race window will not be caught.
matched_golden_ids: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that time.sleep in the test is monkeypatched to a no-op, so the intended wait for flusher threads doesn’t happen, matching the golden concern about restoring sleep or using another sync mechanism.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is dead code — no caller anywhere in the diff or the strategy calls it. The next maintainer hunting restart logic finds two near-identical restart entry points and must determine which is real; the dead one also can't restart a shared process correctly (it would double-assign), so leaving it invites a wrong future call site.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py`, a helper `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is added, but within the shown diff all restart logic uses `_ensure_processes_alive()` which calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. There is no call site in the diff for `_create_process_for_shard`, making it dead/unused code in this change. Leaving an unused, alternate restart entry point alongside `_create_process_for_shards` is a concrete maintainability issue that can confuse future restart logic, even if it doesn't break current behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The two flusher timers use inconsistent tag keys ('shard' vs 'shards') for the same shard identity. Any dashboard/alert querying spans.buffer.flusher.produce by tag 'shard' misses the wait_produce series querying 'shards', so operators tracking per-shard produce latency see split/incomplete data after this deploy.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.main`, the `metrics.timer` for `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` uses `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` while the `metrics.timer` for `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}`. This is a real, diff-grounded inconsistency that will split metric series and can break per-shard dashboards/alerts, but it doesn’t affect functional correctness of flushing itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] join() breaks out of the process loop when the deadline expires and only terminates processes it actually waited on, so remaining flusher processes are never terminated. On shutdown with a short timeout and multiple processes, processes after the first un-waited index keep running (or leak as live spawns) after join() returns, unlike the old single-process path which unconditionally terminated; the consumer shuts down with orphaned flusher processes still polling Redis.

[BUG] The added time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep to a lambda returning None, so the flusher thread gets zero guaranteed time to process after the drift change. test_basic intermittently fails in CI: the flusher thread races the main thread's step.join() with no actual wait, producing flaky failures exactly like the flakiness this sleep was presumably meant to fix.

adjudication.rationale: In `test_basic`, the test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` near the start, and the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` later in the test therefore does nothing (it calls the patched function). So the intended delay to let the flusher run after `current_drift` is changed is not actually provided by this change, making the added line ineffective and potentially leaving the race condition unresolved.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] max_processes=0 (a plausible CLI misconfiguration of --flusher-processes) is silently coerced to 'all shards' by the `max_processes or len(...)` idiom, inverting the operator's intent. An operator setting --flusher-processes 0 to disable the flusher instead gets one process per shard, silently changing resource usage in the opposite direction of the configured value.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, the line `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` will treat an explicitly configured `max_processes=0` (e.g. via the new `--flusher-processes` int option) as falsy and replace it with `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. That silently converts “0” into “all shards” and thus increases process count (`self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))`) in the opposite direction of the provided value. The diff shows no validation preventing 0, and the CLI option is a plain `type=int` with no lower bound.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The entire _ensure_processes_alive restart path (crash detection, per-process restart counter, RuntimeError after MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS, hang detection) has no test coverage in this diff despite being the core of the 'Health Monitoring' in the PR title. A regression in restart logic — e.g. the new isinstance-based kill guard or per-process restart counter — ships undetected; the next engineer changing this code has no executable spec of the health/restart contract.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces substantial new health/restart logic in `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive()` (per-process `process_restarts` dict, hang detection via `process_healthy_since[...]`, crash detection via `is_alive()`/`exitcode`, and restart behavior with an `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` kill guard plus `RuntimeError` after `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`). The added/modified tests (`test_basic`, `test_flusher_processes_limit`, and updating `test_flusher`) only validate shard/process mapping and backpressure bookkeeping, not the restart path or its contract (e.g., triggering a dead process, verifying restart counter increments, verifying `RuntimeError` threshold, or verifying hang-based restarts). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] submit() now calls record_stored_segments() on every per-shard SpansBuffer on every submit, replacing a single call on the shared buffer, without any test asserting the aggregate semantics match the previous single-buffer accounting. If record_stored_segments maintains per-instance state (Redis counters keyed per buffer instance), the restart path in _create_process_for_shards constructs a fresh SpansBuffer that is swapped into self.buffers, dropping that process's accumulated accounting mid-stream; whoever debugs drift/count metrics gets bitten by silently reset counters after each restart.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does change `submit()` from a single `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()` call to iterating `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): buffer.record_stored_segments()` (in `SpanFlusher.submit`). The diff also shows restarts rebuild and replace per-process buffers: `_create_process_for_shards` constructs a fresh `SpansBuffer(shards)` and assigns it into `self.buffers[process_index]`, overwriting any prior instance. However, the claimed impact (dropping accumulated accounting / Redis counters keyed to the buffer instance) depends on `SpansBuffer.record_stored_segments()` maintaining per-instance state, which is not shown in the diff. So the concern is real and diff-grounded as a potential semantics/observability risk and missing coverage, but not a verifiable correctness defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The backpressure MessageRejected check now raises when ANY process exceeds the threshold but the metrics.incr fires once per exceeded process per submit call, changing the metric's emission rate versus the single-process baseline. Existing dashboards/alerts on spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure rate will see N-times-higher counts for the same incident once flusher_processes > 1, tripping rate-based alerts without any alerting change.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.submit`, the new loop over `self.process_backpressure_since.values()` still calls `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure")` at most once per `submit()` call because it immediately `raise MessageRejected()` on the first exceeded threshold (no accumulation over multiple processes). The diff does change semantics to reject when *any* process is backpressured, but it does not emit the backpressure metric N-times per submit based on the number of unhealthy processes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] join() waits sequentially on each process against a shared absolute deadline and breaks out of the loop without terminating or waiting for the remaining processes once the deadline passes. With N flusher processes and a join timeout T, the first slow process consumes the entire T; all subsequent processes are skipped via `break` and never receive terminate(), so spawned processes/thread flushers stay alive past shutdown and any in-flight segments in their shards are dropped — a consumer restart loses data. No test in the diff exercises join() with more than the fast path, so this is unverified.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.join()`, a single absolute `deadline` is computed before `self.next_step.join(timeout)`, so time spent there can exhaust the timeout. The subsequent loop over `self.processes` does `if remaining_time <= 0: break`, which skips waiting on and (critically) skips the `process.terminate()` call for all remaining processes. Thus with multiple flusher processes, some may be left alive past shutdown when the timeout is hit. This is directly visible in the new join logic in `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` in test_basic is a no-op because the test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top of the function, so the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is false and no waiting actually happens. The test passes by racing luck rather than by synchronization: if the flusher threads haven't produced the segment when assertions run, the test flakes; reviewers reading the comment believe the sleep covers the new multiprocess handoff. Note the patched lambda ignores its argument, but it still replaces module-level time.sleep, including this new call.
matched_golden_ids: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify that test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, so the later time.sleep(0.1) call does not actually wait despite being intended as a delay, potentially causing flakiness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit is a structural mirror test: it asserts `flusher.num_processes == 2` and `flusher.max_processes == 2` (echoes of the constructor argument it just passed), never submits or polls a message, and ends with step.join() having verified zero output. The test passes even if the multi-process shard mapping is broken (e.g., shards assigned to the wrong processes, a process flushing nothing, or processes double-flushing a shard) because no behavioral assertion exists — a regression in shard routing or per-process flushing is invisible to it. The only structural check that has any content is total_shards == 4, which is also derivable from the input.

adjudication.rationale: In `test_flusher_processes_limit`, the test passes `flusher_processes=2` into `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory` and then primarily asserts structural echoes of that configuration (`assert flusher.max_processes == 2`, `assert flusher.num_processes == 2`, `assert len(flusher.processes) == 2`). It also checks `total_shards == 4`, which follows directly from `partitions = {Partition(topic, i): 0 for i in range(4)}` and the mapping construction. The test never submits messages to the strategy, never polls, and never asserts any produced output (`messages` is never checked), then ends with `step.join()`. From the diff alone, this means regressions in shard routing or per-process flushing behavior could occur without failing this test, making the finding a concrete, diff-grounded test adequacy concern rather than a product defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The entire rewritten restart path in _ensure_processes_alive — the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError raise, the kill-and-recreate of a shard-group process, and the new per-shard `flusher_unhealthy` metric emission — has no test in the diff that triggers it (no process is killed, no hang simulated, no restart counter incremented in either test file). The highest-risk new logic in the diff (per-process restart bookkeeping, the kill()/isinstance guard, replacing entries in self.processes/self.buffers) ships unverified; checked tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py and test_consumer.py — neither kills a process nor manipulates process_healthy_since. A regression here silently breaks crash recovery in production.

adjudication.rationale: The diff substantially rewrites flusher liveness/restart logic from a single `self.process` to per-shard-group `self.processes` with per-process `process_healthy_since`, `process_backpressure_since`, `process_restarts`, kill/recreate in `_ensure_processes_alive()` and per-shard `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` emissions. The added/updated tests (`test_basic`, `test_flusher_processes_limit`, and the assertion change in `test_flusher.py`) only validate basic flushing behavior and the process/shard mapping/limits; they do not simulate `process.is_alive()==False`, a hang via `process_healthy_since[...]` staleness, nor do they assert restart counter behavior, replacement of entries in `self.processes`/`self.buffers`, or the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS error path. This is a specific, diff-grounded gap in coverage for new high-risk logic, but not a provable defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The backpressure check in submit() now loops over per-process backpressure Values and was verified only by the single-process test_flusher.py assertion `any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())`, which does not distinguish per-process isolation — a backpressure flag stuck on a dead process's Value (whose owning process was replaced but the old Value object kept via process_to_shards_map recreation gap) would still trip the any(). Specifically, when a process is restarted, _create_process_for_shards writes a fresh healthy/backpressure Value into process_healthy_since/process_backpressure_since but nothing ever zeroes the old backpressure Value passed to the killed process; a killed process that had set backpressure_since > 0 leaves a stale Value that permanently raises MessageRejected after backpressure-seconds elapse, and no test covers a restart followed by continued submission.

adjudication.rationale: The finding’s core premise (that a restart creates a *fresh* backpressure/healthy `Value` and leaves an old `Value` behind that continues to trip `submit()`) is not supported by the diff. `process_backpressure_since` and `process_healthy_since` are created once in `__init__` as `mp_context.Value(...)` objects and are **not replaced** on restart; `_create_process_for_shards` only updates `process_healthy_since[process_index].value` and reuses the existing `process_backpressure_since[process_index]` when starting the new process. Therefore there is no “stale old Value object kept” problem as described. While tests don’t cover restart scenarios, the specific defect claimed (permanent MessageRejected due to an orphaned Value) is a misread of the code in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code — no caller in the diff or retained code paths invokes it (restarts go through _create_process_for_shards directly via _ensure_processes_alive). The next maintainer changing shard-to-process mapping must reason about two near-duplicate creation paths; it also performs the wrong restart granularity (restarts one shard's process rather than the whole process group). Deletion candidate.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is introduced but never called: creation happens via `_create_processes()` → `_create_process_for_shards(...)`, and restarts happen in `_ensure_processes_alive()` which also calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. There is no invocation of `_create_process_for_shard` shown, making it dead/unused code and an extra near-duplicate restart path that could confuse future changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The shard-to-process mapping is computed once from buffer.assigned_shards at construction and never updated, so shards added by a Kafka rebalance are never polled by any flusher process. After a partition rebalance that assigns new partitions to this consumer, spans for the new shards are written to Redis but no flusher process ever polls them; segments accumulate in Redis until memory backpressure rejects all messages — silent data stall/loss for those shards until the consumer is restarted.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `SpanFlusher.__init__` computes `process_to_shards_map` once from `buffer.assigned_shards` and then creates per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` instances stored in `self.buffers`. There is no code in the diff that updates this mapping/buffers if shard/partition assignments change later; `_create_process_for_shard` exists but is never invoked. However, the diff does not show whether this processing strategy is recreated on Kafka rebalance (common in consumer frameworks), so the claimed post-rebalance “never polled” behavior cannot be definitively verified from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When buffer.assigned_shards is empty, num_processes is min(max_processes, 0) = 0, so zero flusher processes are created and the flusher has no worker at all. A consumer instantiated with no assigned partitions creates no processes; if partitions are subsequently assigned (the rebalance gap above), there is no flusher to drain Redis, and _ensure_processes_alive iterates an empty dict so no restart/health check ever fires.

adjudication.rationale: In SpanFlusher.__init__, num_processes is computed as min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)). If assigned_shards is empty, this becomes 0, so process_to_shards_map is empty, _create_processes() creates no workers, and _ensure_processes_alive() becomes a no-op because self.processes is empty. That behavior is directly implied by the diff. However, the finding’s claim that partitions are “subsequently assigned” without recreating the flusher/strategy (so Redis would never be drained) is not verifiable from this diff, since rebalance/partition reassignment lifecycle isn’t shown here. This is best treated as an unhandled edge-case/robustness concern rather than a confirmed defect in the shown changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] _create_process_for_shard restarts a process by calling _create_process_for_shards, which spawns a brand-new process and overwrites self.processes[process_index] without joining or reaping the dead/killed old process object, and it is also never called from anywhere (dead code diverging from the restart path in _ensure_processes_alive). Maintainers calling this helper (its name suggests the per-shard restart entry point) get a duplicate process for the same shards alongside the one _ensure_processes_alive manages, causing double-flushing of the same Redis segments and double-producing spans to Kafka; at minimum it is dead code whose presence signals the restart design was left half-refactored.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `_create_process_for_shard`, and it is not referenced anywhere in the shown code paths (restart logic is in `_ensure_processes_alive`, which calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly). The helper also does not terminate/join an existing process before calling `_create_process_for_shards`, and `_create_process_for_shards` overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` with a newly started process. That means if someone were to use this helper as an entry point later, it could leave an old process running for the same shards (risking duplicate flushing/producing). However, since it is dead/uninvoked in this diff, it’s not a currently verifiable runtime defect, but it is a concrete design/maintainability issue introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] join(timeout) consumes the shared deadline across the per-process loop and breaks out on expiry without terminating the remaining processes. On shutdown with a timeout, processes later in the dict are left running (never .terminate()d) while join returns; in the produce_to_pipe=None spawn path those child processes linger holding Redis connections, and any segments still buffered in those shards are never flushed before the consumer exits.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.join()`, a shared `deadline` is computed once, then the method iterates `for process_index, process in self.processes.items()`. If the timeout has expired (`remaining_time <= 0`), it `break`s out of the loop entirely, so any processes later in the dict are neither waited on nor `terminate()`d. Since `terminate()` is only called inside the per-process loop, those remaining `multiprocessing.Process` children can be left running after `join()` returns. This behavior is introduced by the new multi-process `self.processes` handling in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The health-check branch `if not process: continue` is a dead guard — dict values are always Process/Thread objects, never falsy — so the intended 'no process for this index yet' condition it appears to protect against cannot fire. A future refactor that leaves a slot empty (e.g. failed spawn storing None) will silently skip health monitoring for that index with no restart attempted, leaving shards unflushed while the consumer reports healthy.

adjudication.rationale: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the guard `if not process: continue` is effectively unreachable with the code shown: `self.processes` is populated in `_create_process_for_shards` with a started `Process`/`Thread` object (`self.processes[process_index] = process`) and there is no path in the diff that stores `None` or any other falsy sentinel into the dict. So the branch is dead as-written. The rest of the finding (future refactor leaving a slot empty) is speculative, but the dead/unnecessary guard itself is a specific, diff-grounded maintainability issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` only kills `multiprocessing.Process` instances; when `produce_to_pipe` is set the flusher runs as a `threading.Thread`, and a hung thread is left running while `_create_process_for_shards` immediately starts a replacement on the same shards. Two threads poll Redis for the same shards concurrently, so segments can be flushed/produced twice or torn between the old and new thread; the 'unhealthy' condition that triggered the restart is never actually cleared in thread mode, so every subsequent submit() spawns yet another duplicate thread until MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS raises RuntimeError.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive`, the restart path only attempts to stop the old worker when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` (via `process.kill()`), but when `produce_to_pipe` is set the worker is created as a `threading.Thread` in `_create_process_for_shards` (`make_process = threading.Thread`). On a detected hang (`time.time() - process_healthy_since[...] > max_unhealthy_seconds`), `_ensure_processes_alive` will still call `_create_process_for_shards(...)` for that `process_index` without any mechanism to stop/join the existing thread, leaving the old thread potentially running while a new one starts for the same `shards`. That can lead to concurrent flushing/producing for the same shard set (duplicate or interleaved work) and thread leakage. The finding’s additional claim that the unhealthy condition is “never cleared” and thus *every* `submit()` spawns another thread is not strictly guaranteed by the diff (the shared `healthy_since` Value is reset before restart and updated by the new thread), but the core restart-without-stopping-thread issue is directly supported by the changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `join()` breaks out of the process loop when the deadline expires, skipping `process.terminate()` for all remaining processes. On a consumer shutdown where the first process eats the whole join timeout, every remaining flusher process is never terminated and is left running after the consumer's strategy is considered shut down, holding Redis connections and potentially producing duplicate spans; the old single-process code always called terminate after the wait loop.
matched_golden_ids: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug: `join()` exits the loop when the deadline expires, which skips calling `terminate()` on remaining flusher processes, leaving them running after shutdown. This directly matches the golden concern about ensuring termination is attempted even after deadline elapses.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code that starts a new process for a shard's group without killing or joining the existing process stored in `self.processes[process_index]`. Any future caller of this helper (its name invites use in per-shard health handling) silently double-assigns shards to two live processes; the next change to restart logic that reaches for this method introduces duplicate flushing with no error surfaced.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` but nothing in the shown code calls it (restart/health logic uses `_create_process_for_shards` directly inside `_ensure_processes_alive`). As written, `_create_process_for_shard` would indeed start a new process/thread for that shard-group via `_create_process_for_shards` without killing/joining any existing entry in `self.processes[process_index]`, potentially leaving two live workers handling the same shards. However, since it is currently unused, this is not a verifiable runtime defect introduced by the diff, but it is a concrete maintainability/footgun issue grounded in the new code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer uses tag key `"shards"` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` use `"shard"`, both carrying the same `shard_tag` value. Operators dashboarding flusher latency split by shard get wait_produce split into a separate series key from produce, fragmenting the metric family and making the wait-vs-produce comparison silently unjoinable per shard.
matched_golden_ids: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same inconsistency in metric tag keys: `wait_produce` uses `"shards"` while `produce` and `segment_size_bytes` use `"shard"` for the same shard identifier, causing metrics to split into separate series and breaking aggregation/comparison across flush stages.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` builds a brand-new `SpansBuffer(shards)` and overwrites `self.buffers[process_index]`, dropping the old buffer object (and its Redis connection pool) without closing it, and every restart repeats this. A consumer experiencing repeated flusher restarts (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process) leaks one Redis connection pool per restart per process; under the crash-loop conditions this code exists for, the leak compounds exactly when Redis is already under pressure.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shards` a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` is created on every (re)start and stored in `self.buffers[process_index]`, replacing any prior buffer for that process index. In `_ensure_processes_alive` the restart path calls `_create_process_for_shards(...)` after killing the old process, but there is no explicit teardown/close of the previously stored buffer before it is overwritten. The diff alone does not show whether `SpansBuffer` owns resources (e.g., Redis pools) that require explicit closing, so an actual connection-pool leak is not strictly verifiable from the diff, but the resource-lifecycle concern on restart is specific and grounded in the new logic.
